requirements.requirement: Persistent host firewall on node1 permits SSH (22) and TCP 8080
requirements.summary: iptables-save output on node1 shows ACCEPT rules for tcp/22 and tcp/8080 (plus loopback and established/related). Live functional test from node2 shows SSH succeeds and curl to port 8080 returns http_code=200, both before and after a full node1 reboot.

A REJECT catch-all rule follows the allow rules in both IPv4 and IPv6 INPUT chains. A live test connecting to an unrelated port (9999) fails with 'No route to host' both pre- and post-reboot, directly demonstrating the reject behavior.

An Ansible inventory and playbook (host-firewall.yml) were authored on the control node (node2) and executed with ansible-playbook against node1 using ansible.builtin.iptables and community.general.apk modules; a second run confirms idempotency (all tasks reported 'ok').

Rules were saved to /etc/iptables/rules-save and rules6-save and the iptables/ip6tables OpenRC services were enabled at the default runlevel. A full reboot of node1 was performed and observed end-to-end: pre-restart boot_id (6d15d99d) and healthy baseline were captured, the reboot was acknowledged, a changed post-restart boot_id (cfef943e) was confirmed, and the iptables rules plus SSH/8080-allow/9999-reject functional behavior were shown restored automatically without any manual reconfiguration.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node (node1 and node2)
requirements.summary: Both node1 and node2 show a coherent pre-restart baseline (boot_id, service/rule state), a restart acknowledgement, a distinct post-restart boot_id, and recovered service state (node1: sshd/iptables/ip6tables and firewall behavior; node2: SSH and Ansible functionality restored, connectivity to node1 confirmed). This matches the fixed before-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots showing node1 6d15d99d→cfef943e and node2 416c5cf5→4ce6264c.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied all material outcomes of the task: a persistent, Ansible-managed iptables/ip6tables firewall on node1 allows SSH and TCP 8080 while rejecting all other inbound traffic, and this was directly verified functionally both before and after a full reboot of node1, with matching boot-identity changes confirming a real restart. The separately mandated node-restart evidence protocol was also completed coherently for both node1 and node2, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. Minor hygiene concerns are a necessary but unreverted root-account unlock on node1 and a small leftover /tmp/reboot.log file.
limitations: Root-account unlock on node1 (passwd -u root) was required to establish SSH/Ansible connectivity given the environment's locked default state, but this is a security-relevant, non-reverted change outside the immediate firewall scope.
A trivial temp file (/tmp/reboot.log) remained on node1 after the reboot helper; low-risk but not cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands are directly tied to the task: installing iptables/ip6tables/python3 (needed prerequisites, retained), writing and applying the Ansible playbook, and bounded diagnostic HTTP/nc listeners on 8080/9999 that were cleaned up after use (cmd-3bcf223d6bfc4d39, cmd-1b222b25f54f4de2). Two items are worth flagging: (1) the executor ran `passwd -u root` on node1 to unlock the root account (cmd-f46cee930cfc4f6d) because root login was otherwise locked, blocking pubkey auth; this was a necessary prerequisite to establish Ansible/SSH connectivity but is a persistent security-relevant change (root login unlocked) that was not reverted. (2) A minor residual file /tmp/reboot.log was left on node1 after the reboot helper command (cmd-7ee0efa426ce421a), visible in the after-executor temporary-files diff — low-risk and small, but not cleaned up. No failed/conflicting services, no destructive or broad mutations, and no unnecessary experiments outside the task's causal chain were observed.
